title: Renewing renewables the next chapter in the energy transition
gist: Wood Mackenzie's Horizons report argues that decommissioning and repowering of more than 2.5 TW of ageing wind and solar in the 2040s will make renewal as big an installation driver as new build, lifting equipment sales 60%+ by 2050 even as net additions fall. Repowering raises output from better sites and technology, which weakens capacity targets that ignore retirements, depresses long-run power prices (Germany -12-19% in the 2040s), and turns prime operating sites into acquisition targets.

insights.claim: More than 3.5 TW (AC) of wind and solar capacity was operating globally by end-2025, and Wood Mackenzie forecasts more than 2.5 TW of it will face an abandon, life-extend or repower decision in the 2040s.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: End-of-life renewables create a multi-TW replacement cycle that should be in long-range demand models.
insights.locator: We forecast that more than 2.5 terawatts

insights.claim: Unlike an oil or gas well, a wind or solar site never exhausts its resource; only the equipment ages, either through physical wear or technological obsolescence, so the site itself keeps value.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Value renewable assets as perpetual sites with periodic equipment refresh, not depleting assets.
insights.quote: Unlike an oil or gas well, a wind or solar site never exhausts its resource.
insights.locator: Unlike an oil or gas well

insights.claim: Wind turbines typically have a 20-year design life; more than 30 GW of wind will have been decommissioned worldwide by end-2026, two-thirds of it between 2022 and 2026.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Wind decommissioning is already accelerating, so repowering demand is emerging now.
insights.locator: Wind decommissioning is already happening

insights.claim: Almost 50 GW of wind capacity has operated for more than 20 years as of 2026, rising to over 230 GW by 2040 and perhaps 440 GW by 2050; solar's over-20-year fleet will overtake wind's before 2040.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: The addressable repowering pool grows roughly ninefold by 2050, with solar joining at scale in the late 2030s.
insights.locator: This considerable increase in wind decommissioning

insights.claim: Repower-vs-extend decisions come down to comparing the NPV of extending the existing project's life, including technical and non-technical factors, against fully repowering it.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Any shift in power prices, subsidies or equipment costs changes the timing of the replacement wave.
insights.locator: An owner’s decision to decommission wind or solar equipment

insights.claim: Solar modules carry 25-30 year warranties, but because solar technology has turned over roughly every other year for the past decade, solar assets are often repowered before their design life ends so owners can capture new technology rather than repair.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Fast tech cycles pull forward solar replacement demand, supporting module OEM volumes.
insights.locator: Solar modules are sold with 25- to 30-year warranties

insights.claim: Rapid solar technology change makes spare parts for older plants hard to find, and component repair is more common in distributed solar than in utility-scale projects.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Parts obsolescence pushes older utility-scale solar toward full repowering rather than O&M life extension.
insights.locator: In a repowering context

insights.claim: A single wind turbine can be up to 15 MW and cost 800,000 times more than a 300 W solar panel, so wind owners run fuller O&M programmes with key component replacement that can extend life beyond design life, sometimes outlasting solar.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Wind life-extension services (major component replacement) are a distinct revenue pool from solar.
insights.locator: Wind as a technology is also structurally different to solar

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie has tracked 25,000 decommissioned wind turbines and applies project-level lifetime assumptions by turbine technology, owner type and market, including rising average lifespans over time.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: The forecast rests on a large empirical base of real retirements, not only design-life assumptions.
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie has tracked 25,000 decommissioned wind turbines

insights.claim: Repowering competes for the same offtake contracts and subsidies as greenfield with similar capex and opex, so its edge is mainly higher output and faster market access, since it skips grid-connection waits and moves faster through permitting.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Interconnected operating sites carry a speed and yield premium in queue-constrained markets.
insights.locator: A repowering project generally competes for the same offtake contracts

insights.claim: German wind sites decommissioned this decade have wind speeds on average 4% higher than new greenfield projects (up to 30%), and a 4% wind-speed gain gives about 7% higher capacity factor and 7% lower LCOE.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: The oldest wind sites hold the best resource; repowering them beats new sites on cost.
insights.locator: For example, the wind speeds of the sites that have been decommissioned in Germany

insights.claim: Increasing capacity during repowering is often blocked by permitting and grid limits, so capacity usually stays the same and the gains come from higher energy output per MW.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Model repowering upside as a generation (GWh) uplift, not a capacity increase.
insights.locator: The fundamental aim of repowering

insights.claim: Average wind turbine rating has risen from 1.5 MW in 2006 to 6 MW in 2026 and is forecast to reach 7.5 MW by 2036, so the net number of turbines added is declining even as capacity grows.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Repowering replaces many small turbines with few large ones, so supplier revenue follows MW rather than unit count.
insights.locator: Wind turbines and solar modules have become significantly more efficient

insights.claim: Solar module efficiencies rose 69% on average between 2005 and 2025, available technology could raise cell efficiency by more than 50% to 2045, and today's solar sites are often up to 30% smaller than 2010 sites for the same capacity.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Repowered solar sites can add output on the same land, raising the value of existing permitted footprints.
insights.locator: The same applies to solar

insights.claim: Wind turbine design life has climbed from 20 to more than 30 years with 97% post-degradation time-based availability, while solar warranties rose from 25 to 30 years and year-25 degradation improved 9% over the past decade.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Newer fleets will retire later, so the replacement cycle after the 2040s may be spread out and slower.
insights.locator: Turbines and modules are not just getting more efficient

insights.claim: Governments set renewable targets in megawatts of capacity but rarely account for decommissioning, which makes already ambitious targets harder and will weigh more on 2030s targets.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Expect systematic target misses and possible new repowering incentives as a policy catalyst.
insights.locator: Governments frequently set renewable supply targets

insights.claim: The European Commission's 500 GW wind target for 2030 needs about 37 GW a year of additions from 2023-2030; with 17 GW expected to be decommissioned, an extra 2 GW a year is needed, and the sector is already falling short.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: The EU wind target is unlikely to be met; watch for policy responses that support European turbine demand.
insights.locator: The European Commission, for example, has targeted 500 GW

insights.claim: Assuming retiring German capacity is replaced at the same capacity factor ignores degradation and repowering gains; Wood Mackenzie calculates these raise German onshore wind post-curtailment output by 16% in 2050, about one-third of Germany's current wind generation or Portugal's entire power demand.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Consensus German wind supply forecasts may be too low, with bearish implications for long-dated power prices.
insights.locator: In Europe’s largest power market, Germany

insights.claim: Repowering-driven output gains would cut German power prices by 12-19% in the 2040s, all else equal, creating downside for projects whose 10-25 year revenue contracts expire into merchant or corporate PPA exposure.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Haircut post-contract tail values in renewable IPP and yieldco valuations.
insights.quote: The gains from repowering could create downside risk to post-contract revenue on those projects if nothing else changes
insights.locator: Most wind and solar projects built today have contracts

insights.claim: Global wind and solar capacity additions will decline in 2026, and without repowering the decline would continue because of weaker US policy support, high decarbonisation already reached in Europe, and grid-integration limits in China.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: New-build growth is stalling in the three largest markets, so replacement demand is the key support for suppliers.
insights.locator: Without repowering, annual new solar and wind installations would decline

insights.claim: Although annual net wind and solar additions will fall gradually through 2050, equipment sales in 2050 will be more than 60% higher than in 2026 because ageing equipment must be replaced.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Counter to the 'peak renewables' narrative, turbine and module OEMs have a long replacement-driven growth tail.
insights.locator: Repowering will ensure that wind and solar remain a growth business

insights.claim: Decommissioning will drive 44% of wind and 23% of solar buildout in the 2040s, more than 70% of installations in Europe's established markets, and as little as 1% in new Asian markets.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Early-adopter markets become replacement-dominated; supplier growth there depends on renewal cycles.
insights.locator: Some 44% and 23%, respectively

insights.claim: Year-to-year swings in decommissioning volumes will complicate supplier planning and government efforts to build domestic manufacturing, and depending on economic nationalism and energy security, sites may be repowered with a different technology than originally installed.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Replacement demand is lumpy, and technology switching at repowered sites could redistribute share among suppliers.
insights.locator: Year-to-year uncertainty in the level of decommissioning

insights.claim: In the 2040s global power demand growth is forecast to slow while wind and solar installations rise because of decommissioning, with the era of renewal expected to produce more installations than ever before.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Renewable installation volumes decouple from demand growth; don't size supplier markets on load growth alone.
insights.quote: we are expecting the era of renewal to lead to more installations than ever before
insights.locator: We are set to enter a new chapter in the energy transition

insights.claim: For ageing renewables, long-term value increasingly lies in the site (grid connection, resource quality, access, prior zoning, community support), fuelling a strategy of buying operating projects in prime locations to tear down and rebuild.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Operating-asset M&A should price optionality on the site, not just remaining equipment cash flows.
insights.locator: Repowering shifts the entry point for asset owners

insights.claim: Buy-and-repower strategies will spread fastest where land and grid capacity are scarce or local support for new projects is low, led by Europe and the US, and fragmented small, privately owned fleets in Germany and France could accelerate consolidation.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Roll-up opportunities in German and French small-scale wind and solar for consolidators with repowering capability.
insights.locator: This will become increasingly common in markets with limited land availability

insights.claim: Winning repowering investments depends on timing: finding sites where revenue forecasts and policy align with a seller who underrates the value or lacks the capability to act; incumbents must estimate residual value to choose between sell, extend or repower.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: An information-edge play: target owners without repowering expertise.
insights.quote: a willing seller who doesn’t recognise the value or lacks the capabilities to seize these opportunities
insights.locator: Successful investment will be about timing

insights.claim: Turbine and module OEMs could gain more work, and in some cases equity stakes, from ageing fleets if they get better at estimating residual life and extending assets efficiently.
insights.speaker: Søren Lassen
insights.so_what: Watch OEMs building lifecycle and service analytics as a route into asset ownership.
insights.locator: For the major solar module and turbine original equipment manufacturers
